summary.text: Long-grain white rice usually uses 2 parts liquid to 1 part rice, and it roughly triples in volume when cooked.

storage.text: Keep uncooked white rice in a cool, dry place in a tightly closed container.
Milled white rice keeps almost indefinitely on the pantry shelf if stored properly.
Refrigerate cooked rice within 2 hours, or within 1 hour above 90°F.
Cooked rice keeps 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator at 40°F or below.
Cool cooked rice to 70°F within two hours, then to 40°F within an additional four hours.
Cooked rice can be frozen up to six months.

preparation.text: Do not rinse enriched white rice, since rinsing removes nutrients.
American-grown rice does not need washing or rinsing before cooking.
Use a pot large enough, since rice triples in volume.

substitutions.name: U.S. basmati, white
substitutions.note: USA Rice's chart lists 2 parts liquid and 15 to 18 minutes for this white rice.

substitutions.name: Medium-grain white rice
substitutions.note: Use 1 1/2 parts liquid per part of rice, per the USA Rice chart.

substitutions.name: Short-grain white rice
substitutions.note: Use 1 1/4 parts liquid per part of rice, per the USA Rice chart.

substitutions.name: Other white rice types
substitutions.note: Liquid needs can differ slightly by rice type.

safety.text: Refrigerate cooked rice promptly; Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking.
Do not leave cooked rice on the counter for long periods while it cools.
Rice can look and smell normal even when toxins are present.
Putting rice back in the refrigerator does not reset the 2-hour limit.

why.text: Rice cookers make white rice easy and foolproof, and they keep it warm.

steps.text: Follow the manufacturer's directions for combining the rice and liquid.
Turn the cooker on and select white rice.
The cooker switches off on its own once it senses the temperature and moisture change.
Fluff with a fork or slotted spoon once cooked.

doneness.text: The cooker stops automatically when the rice has absorbed the liquid.

why.text: Choose the stovetop when you want the standard method, at 2 parts liquid to 1 part long-grain rice.

quantities.label: Liquid per cup of long-grain rice
Montana: water per cup of rice

steps.text: Combine rice, liquid, salt, and butter in a 2- to 3-quart saucepan.
Heat to boiling and stir once or twice.
Reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and simmer.
Simmer 15 to 18 minutes for long-grain white rice.
Remove from the heat and fluff with a fork.

tips.text: Do not stir the rice; stirring releases starch and makes it sticky.
Keep the lid on while it cooks so steam does not escape.
If the rice is crunchy, add more liquid, cover, and keep cooking.

doneness.text: Cook 2 to 4 minutes longer if the rice is not tender or the liquid is not absorbed.
Rice is done when the liquid is gone.

why.text: Choose the microwave when you want rice in about 25 minutes, per Montana's long-grain note.

steps.text: Combine the rice, liquid, salt, and butter in a 2½- to 3-quart deep microwave-safe baking dish and cover tightly.
Microwave on high for five minutes or until boiling.
Reduce to medium power and microwave 15 minutes, or until the water is absorbed.

tips.text: Microwave wattages differ, so follow your oven's directions.
Montana gives 10 minutes high then 15 minutes medium-low for long-grain rice.

doneness.text: Done when the water is absorbed.
